title: Fioricet and Alcohol: Why the Mix Is Dangerous (Barbiturate Risk)
excerpt: Fioricet contains butalbital, a barbiturate, plus acetaminophen. Why mixing it with alcohol can dangerously slow breathing, strain your liver, and when to call 911.
metaDescription: Fioricet contains a barbiturate and acetaminophen. Why mixing it with alcohol is dangerous, why never to take it for a hangover, and when to call 911.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The honest answer first:** don't drink alcohol while you're taking Fioricet. Fioricet contains butalbital, which is a barbiturate, a type of sedative that slows down your brain and your breathing. Alcohol does the same thing, and the two add to each other. Together they can cause extreme drowsiness, confusion, dangerously slow breathing, and in the worst cases coma or death. Fioricet also contains acetaminophen (the drug in Tylenol), which puts extra strain on a liver that is already busy with alcohol. The prescribing information for butalbital products warns that alcohol and other sedatives add to their effects, so this isn't a gray area.

**The quick rules:** Don't drink at all while you're taking Fioricet, and ask your prescriber or pharmacist when it's safe to drink again after your last dose. Never take Fioricet for a hangover headache. Never take an extra dose because you've been drinking and the headache got worse. If you already mixed the two, don't drive, don't drink any more, don't take another dose until you've talked to a pharmacist, and stay with someone who can keep an eye on your breathing. If someone is very hard to wake, breathing slowly or noisily, or has blue or gray lips, call 911.

> **This is not medical advice.** This article explains how Fioricet and alcohol interact based on the official prescribing information and general research. It is not a substitute for your doctor or pharmacist, who know your dose, your other medicines, and your health history. **Don't drink alcohol while taking Fioricet**, and don't stop it suddenly on your own if you've been taking it regularly; talk to your prescriber first. **Call 911 right away if** someone who took Fioricet and alcohol is hard to wake, breathing slowly or shallowly, making gurgling or snoring sounds they can't be woken from, has a seizure, or has blue or gray lips or fingertips. In the US you can also call Poison Control at **1-800-222-1222** at any hour, including if you think too much acetaminophen was taken.

## What Fioricet Actually Is

Fioricet is a prescription headache medicine. It's mainly prescribed for tension headaches, the kind that feel like a tight band around your head. Each standard capsule combines three drugs:

1. **Butalbital (50 mg).** A barbiturate. It relaxes muscles and calms the nervous system. This is the part that makes Fioricet sedating, and the part that makes it dangerous with alcohol.
2. **Acetaminophen (300 mg).** The same pain reliever that's in Tylenol. It's processed by the liver, and alcohol changes how safely the liver can handle it.
3. **Caffeine (40 mg).** About the amount in a small cup of tea or half a cup of coffee. It helps the pain relievers work and narrows blood vessels in the head.

You may also see the same combination sold under other brand names, or as generic "butalbital, acetaminophen, and caffeine" tablets or capsules. There are close relatives too:

- **Fiorinal** uses aspirin instead of acetaminophen, along with butalbital and caffeine.
- **Fioricet with Codeine** and **Fiorinal with Codeine** add codeine, an opioid. That adds a second strong sedative to the mix and makes alcohol even more dangerous.
- **Butalbital and acetaminophen** without caffeine is also available.

Everything in this guide about butalbital and alcohol applies to all of these. If your bottle says "butalbital" anywhere on it, treat alcohol as off-limits.

## Why Fioricet and Alcohol Are a Dangerous Mix

There are two separate problems here. The first, sedation and slowed breathing, is the one that can kill quickly. The second, liver strain, builds over time and with higher doses.

### Problem 1: Two sedatives stacking on the same brain system

Your brain uses a chemical messenger called **GABA** to calm activity down. It works through receptors (think of them as docking stations on nerve cells) called GABA-A receptors. When GABA docks there, it opens a small channel that quiets the nerve cell.

Barbiturates like butalbital make those receptors respond more strongly and keep the channel open longer. At higher levels, barbiturates can open the channel even without GABA present. Alcohol also boosts GABA-A signaling, along with blocking some of the brain's "go" signals.

So when you drink on Fioricet, two drugs are pressing down on the same brakes at once. The effects don't just sit side by side; they add together, and they can be stronger than you'd expect from either one alone. This is the same reason doctors warn so strongly about mixing alcohol with benzodiazepines like Xanax, which work on the same receptors. (Our guide to [Xanax and alcohol](/never-hungover/xanax-and-alcohol) covers that related interaction.)

What that stacking can look like:

- Much heavier drowsiness and "drunkenness" than the amount you drank would normally cause
- Slurred speech, poor coordination, stumbling, and falls
- Confusion and memory gaps
- Slow or shallow breathing
- In serious cases, being impossible to wake, coma, or breathing that stops

Barbiturates have a narrower safety margin than many newer sedatives, meaning the gap between a dose that works and a dose that harms is smaller. That's a big part of why doctors use them far less than they once did, and why adding alcohol is treated so seriously.

### Why caffeine doesn't cancel it out

People sometimes assume the caffeine in Fioricet will balance out the drowsiness. It won't. Caffeine can make you feel more alert, but it doesn't speed up how your body clears butalbital or alcohol, and it doesn't protect your breathing. If anything, feeling a little more awake can make it harder to notice how impaired you are, which can lead someone to drink more or decide they're fine to drive. The same "wide-awake drunk" problem is why mixing energy drinks with alcohol is a concern; we cover that in [caffeine and alcohol](/never-hungover/caffeine-and-alcohol).

### Butalbital lasts a long time

Butalbital isn't a short-acting drug. The prescribing information lists its plasma half-life at about 35 hours. Half-life is the time it takes your body to clear half of a dose, so a meaningful amount can still be in your system a day or more after you take it, and longer if you've taken several doses in a row.

This matters for two reasons:

- **"I took it this morning, so I can drink tonight" is not safe thinking.** The butalbital from a morning dose is still very much active that evening.
- **Repeated doses build up.** If you've taken Fioricet over a few days, levels can be higher than after a single dose.

How long you should wait after your last dose before drinking depends on your dose, how often you've been taking it, your age, and how well your liver and kidneys work. That's a question for your prescriber or pharmacist, not something to work out on your own.

### Problem 2: Acetaminophen and your liver

The acetaminophen in Fioricet brings a second, slower risk. Your liver breaks down most of each acetaminophen dose safely, but a small share is turned into a toxic by-product called **NAPQI**. Normally your liver neutralizes NAPQI right away with an antioxidant called **glutathione**.

Regular heavy drinking tips that balance in the wrong direction. It increases the liver enzyme (called CYP2E1) that produces NAPQI, and it lowers glutathione stores. Skipping meals lowers glutathione too. When NAPQI is made faster than glutathione can clean it up, liver cells are damaged. Acetaminophen is the leading cause of acute liver failure in the United States, and many of those cases are accidental, often involving more than one acetaminophen product and often alcohol.

Prescription combination products that contain acetaminophen carry a boxed warning, the FDA's strongest kind, about the risk of serious liver injury. The FDA also limited the amount of acetaminophen in each pill of prescription combination products to 325 mg to lower the chance of accidental overdose.

Barbiturates add one more wrinkle: they're known to ramp up some of the liver's drug-processing enzymes over time. The prescribing information for butalbital products notes this enzyme effect, and it's one more reason the label tells people not to combine these drugs with alcohol and to be careful with any other acetaminophen.

For the full explanation of how acetaminophen and alcohol interact, see our guide to [Tylenol and alcohol](/never-hungover/tylenol-and-alcohol).

### The hidden acetaminophen trap

Because Fioricet already contains acetaminophen, it's easy to go over the daily limit without realizing it. That's especially true after drinking, when you might reach for:

- Tylenol or store-brand acetaminophen for a headache
- A "nighttime" or PM product to help you sleep (many contain acetaminophen; see [Tylenol PM and alcohol](/never-hungover/tylenol-pm-and-alcohol))
- Cold and flu medicines, many of which list acetaminophen as "APAP" or "acetaminophen" on the label
- Excedrin, which also contains acetaminophen (see [Excedrin and alcohol](/never-hungover/excedrin-and-alcohol))

Don't take any other acetaminophen product while you're on Fioricet unless your prescriber or pharmacist has told you exactly how much is safe in total. Follow the daily limit on your prescription label, and never take more Fioricet than prescribed.

## Never Use Fioricet for a Hangover

This deserves its own section, because it's an easy mistake to make. You wake up after drinking with a pounding headache, and there's a bottle of headache pills in the cabinet. Don't take Fioricet.

Here's why the morning after is an especially bad time:

- **Alcohol may still be in your blood.** After a heavy night, you may not be fully sober the next morning. Adding a barbiturate on top of leftover alcohol brings back the stacking-sedation risk described above.
- **Your liver is already working.** It's still processing alcohol, you may not have eaten, and glutathione stores may be low. That's a poor time to add acetaminophen.
- **It's not what Fioricet is for.** A hangover headache comes from dehydration, poor sleep, inflammation, and the by-products of alcohol breakdown. Fioricet is prescribed for tension headaches, and using a sedative to manage a hangover can set up a cycle of reaching for it more often.
- **Withdrawal can be part of it.** For people who drink heavily, the next day can involve early alcohol withdrawal, which already lowers the seizure threshold. Barbiturates should never be used to self-manage alcohol withdrawal outside medical care.

If you have a hangover headache, the safer basics are water, food, rest, and time. Once the alcohol has fully cleared and you've eaten, a single label dose of an over-the-counter pain reliever may help, as long as you're not taking other medicines that conflict with it. Our guides to [Advil or Tylenol for a hangover](/never-hungover/advil-or-tylenol-for-hangover) and [hangover headache relief](/never-hungover/hangover-headache-fast-relief-methods-2025) cover the options. If you're already on Fioricet, ask your pharmacist which pain reliever is safe for you, because the acetaminophen count matters.

## If You've Already Mixed Fioricet and Alcohol

If you've had a drink and taken Fioricet, or the other way around, here's what to do. This isn't a guide to how much is "okay." It's how to stay safe right now.

1. **Stop.** Don't drink any more alcohol and don't take another dose of Fioricet or any other sedating medicine.
2. **Don't drive or operate anything.** Not a car, a bike, a scooter, or machinery. Your reaction time and judgment are affected even if you feel alert.
3. **Call a pharmacist or Poison Control.** In the US, Poison Control is **1-800-222-1222**, free and open 24 hours. Tell them what you took, how much, when, and how much you drank. They can tell you whether you need to be seen.
4. **Don't be alone.** Have someone stay with you who knows what you took and can check on your breathing and how easily you wake up.
5. **Don't take anything else to "balance it out."** No extra coffee, energy drinks, sleep aids, or other pain relievers. They won't reverse the sedation, and some add more risk.
6. **Know when to call 911.** Use the signs in the next section.

If you're looking after someone else who has mixed the two and is very drowsy, keep them on their side (the recovery position) so they won't choke if they vomit, and keep checking that you can wake them.

## Emergency Signs: When to Call 911

Call 911 right away if someone who has taken Fioricet (or any butalbital product) and alcohol shows any of these:

- **Can't be woken up**, or wakes only briefly and drifts off again
- **Slow, shallow, or irregular breathing**, or pauses in breathing
- **Gurgling, choking, or deep snoring sounds** while unresponsive
- **Blue or gray lips, fingertips, or skin**
- **Cold, clammy skin**
- **A seizure**
- **Severe confusion** or not making sense
- **Very slow heartbeat** or fainting

While you wait for help:

- Stay with them.
- Turn them on their side if they're very drowsy or vomiting.
- Don't give them food, drinks, coffee, or more medicine.
- If you know they also took an opioid (for example, Fioricet with Codeine) and you have naloxone (Narcan), use it as directed. Naloxone reverses opioids, not barbiturates or alcohol, but it can still help if an opioid is part of the picture, and it won't harm someone who hasn't taken one.
- Tell the 911 operator and paramedics exactly what was taken and when. Bring the medicine bottle if you can.

### Liver warning signs (can show up later)

An acetaminophen overdose often causes few symptoms at first. Early signs can look like a hangover: nausea, vomiting, sweating, and feeling unwell. Later signs include pain under the right ribs, yellow skin or eyes, dark urine, and confusion. If there's any chance too much acetaminophen was taken, call Poison Control at **1-800-222-1222** right away, even if the person feels fine. The hospital antidote works best when it's given early.

## Who Is at Higher Risk

Mixing Fioricet and alcohol is dangerous for everyone, but some people are at even greater risk:

- **Older adults**, who tend to clear medicines more slowly and are more likely to fall
- **People taking other sedating medicines**, such as opioids, benzodiazepines, sleep pills, gabapentin, muscle relaxers, or sedating antihistamines. Each one adds to the sedation. See our guides to [muscle relaxers and alcohol](/never-hungover/muscle-relaxers-and-alcohol) and [gabapentin and alcohol](/never-hungover/gabapentin-and-alcohol).
- **People with sleep apnea, asthma, COPD, or other breathing problems**, because barbiturates and alcohol both slow breathing
- **People with liver disease** or a history of high liver enzymes
- **People who drink heavily most days**, because of the liver effects described above and the risk of withdrawal
- **People taking Fioricet often or at higher doses**, because butalbital builds up and the body can become dependent on it
- **Anyone who is pregnant or breastfeeding**, who should talk to their doctor about headache treatment in general

If any of these apply to you, it's worth having a direct conversation with your prescriber about alcohol, even if you've been told the general warning before.

## Dependence, Rebound Headaches, and Why Doctors Limit Fioricet

Butalbital can be habit-forming. With regular use, your body adjusts to it, and stopping suddenly after frequent use can cause withdrawal. Barbiturate withdrawal can be serious, with symptoms like anxiety, shaking, trouble sleeping, and in some cases seizures. That's why the label advice is not to stop on your own if you've been taking it regularly, but to work out a plan with your prescriber.

There's a second issue that's specific to headaches. Taking headache medicines too often can cause **medication overuse headache**, sometimes called rebound headache. The medicine relieves today's headache but helps set up tomorrow's, and the headaches become more frequent over time. Butalbital combinations are among the medicines most closely linked to this problem.

For those reasons, headache specialists generally treat butalbital products as a last resort, especially for migraine. The American Headache Society's recommendations through the Choosing Wisely campaign advise against using butalbital-containing medicines for migraine except as a last resort. Many doctors now prefer other options for tension headaches and migraines.

Alcohol fits into this picture in a few ways. It can trigger headaches and migraines on its own (we cover that in [migraine after drinking](/never-hungover/migraine-after-drinking)), it disrupts sleep, which can make headaches more frequent, and it adds to the sedation of butalbital. If you find yourself needing Fioricet often, or headaches seem to cluster after drinking, that's a good reason to see your doctor about the overall pattern rather than reaching for more medicine.

This guide isn't about alcohol use or recovery. If you're worried about how much you drink, or about how often you use Fioricet, your doctor is the right person to talk to, and they can help without judgment.

## Safer Ways to Handle Headaches if You Drink Sometimes

If you're on Fioricet and you know there's an event coming up where you'd usually drink, the time to plan is beforehand, not on the night.

- **Ask your prescriber directly.** Say something like, "I have a wedding in two weeks. When would I need to stop Fioricet beforehand, and how long after should I wait before taking it again?" They can give you an answer based on your dose and health.
- **Ask about alternatives.** If you have occasional headaches and drink socially, there may be a treatment that fits your life better. Many headache medicines don't involve a barbiturate.
- **Keep a headache diary.** Note headaches, sleep, food, drinks, and medicines. Patterns, like headaches the day after drinking, are useful for your doctor and can point to simpler fixes.
- **Cover the basics.** Regular sleep, steady meals, hydration, and managing stress all help with tension headaches.
- **Don't keep Fioricet in the same place as party supplies.** It sounds minor, but making it a deliberate choice rather than a reflex helps avoid a 2 a.m. mistake.

The simplest rule is the safest: if you've taken Fioricet, don't drink. If you've been drinking, don't take Fioricet. When in doubt about timing, ask a pharmacist. They can answer quickly, and it's free.

## What About DHM and Other Supplements?

DHM (dihydromyricetin) is a plant compound that this site covers in depth for hangover support. It has interesting research on how the body handles alcohol, but most of that research comes from animal studies, and human data are limited.

To be very clear: **there's no good evidence that DHM, or any other supplement, makes it safe to drink while taking Fioricet.** No supplement has been shown to reverse barbiturate sedation, protect breathing, or prevent acetaminophen liver damage from this combination. Don't use any supplement as a reason to combine them.

If you take any prescription medicine, including Fioricet, check with your pharmacist before adding supplements. Our [DHM medication interactions guide](/never-hungover/dhm-medication-interactions-safety-guide-2025) and our broader guide to [alcohol and medications](/never-hungover/alcohol-and-medications) are good places to read more, but your pharmacist knows your full list.

## Fioricet Compared With Other Medicines That Clash With Alcohol

It can help to see where Fioricet sits among other common medicines:

| Medicine | Main risk with alcohol | Official advice |
|---|---|---|
| Fioricet (butalbital + acetaminophen + caffeine) | Stacked sedation and slowed breathing, plus liver strain | Avoid alcohol; ask prescriber about timing |
| Fiorinal (butalbital + aspirin + caffeine) | Stacked sedation, plus stomach bleeding risk from aspirin | Avoid alcohol; ask prescriber about timing |
| Opioids such as [oxycodone](/never-hungover/oxycodone-and-alcohol) or [tramadol](/never-hungover/tramadol-and-alcohol) | Stacked sedation and slowed breathing | Boxed warning; avoid alcohol |
| Benzodiazepines such as Xanax | Stacked sedation and slowed breathing | Boxed warning about combining with opioids; avoid alcohol |
| Tylenol (acetaminophen) alone | Liver strain, mainly with heavy regular drinking or high doses | Label warning for 3+ drinks a day; ask a doctor |

The pattern is simple. Any medicine that slows the brain is dangerous with alcohol, and Fioricet does that while also carrying acetaminophen's liver warning. It belongs in the strictest category.

## The Bottom Line

- **Fioricet contains a barbiturate (butalbital).** With alcohol, it can cause dangerous sedation, slowed breathing, coma, or death.
- **It also contains acetaminophen,** which adds liver strain, especially with heavy drinking, fasting, or other acetaminophen products.
- **Butalbital lasts a long time,** with a half-life of around 35 hours, so a morning dose is still active that night.
- **Never take Fioricet for a hangover,** and never take extra because you've been drinking.
- **Ask your prescriber or pharmacist** when it's safe to drink after your last dose. Don't guess.
- **Call 911** if someone is hard to wake, breathing slowly, or has blue or gray lips. Call Poison Control at **1-800-222-1222** for any possible acetaminophen overdose, even without symptoms.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Can you drink alcohol while taking Fioricet?**

No. Fioricet contains butalbital, a barbiturate, and alcohol adds to its sedating effect on the brain and breathing. The combination can cause extreme drowsiness, confusion, dangerously slow breathing, and in serious cases coma or death. Fioricet's acetaminophen also adds strain on the liver. Don't drink while you're taking it, and ask your prescriber or pharmacist when it's safe to drink again after your last dose.

**Is one drink on Fioricet dangerous?**

It can be. There's no amount of alcohol known to be safe with butalbital. Your dose, how recently you took it, how many doses you've taken, your age, and any other sedating medicines all change the risk. The official advice is to avoid alcohol. If you've already had one drink, don't have more, don't drive, and ask a pharmacist before your next dose.

**How long after taking Fioricet can I drink?**

There's no single waiting period that fits everyone, and it's not something to work out yourself. Butalbital's half-life is about 35 hours, so it stays in your system well into the next day, and longer after repeated doses. Ask your prescriber or pharmacist when it's safe to drink after your last dose.

**Can I take Fioricet for a hangover headache?**

No. The morning after drinking, alcohol may still be in your blood, which brings back the sedation risk, and your liver is already busy, which makes the acetaminophen riskier. Fioricet is a prescription medicine for tension headaches and should only be used as prescribed. For a hangover headache, start with water, food, and rest. Ask your pharmacist which over-the-counter pain reliever is safe for you, especially if you have Fioricet in your system.

**What are the signs of a Fioricet and alcohol overdose?**

Warning signs include being very hard to wake, slow or shallow breathing, gurgling or deep snoring sounds, blue or gray lips, cold clammy skin, severe confusion, a slow heartbeat, and seizures. Call 911 right away, keep the person on their side, and stay with them. Liver damage from acetaminophen can show up later, so call Poison Control (1-800-222-1222 in the US) for any possible overdose even if the person seems fine.

**Can I take Tylenol with Fioricet after drinking?**

Don't take extra Tylenol or any other acetaminophen product with Fioricet unless your prescriber or pharmacist has told you it's safe, because Fioricet already contains acetaminophen. Doubling up is a common way people accidentally go over the daily limit, and drinking makes that more dangerous for your liver. Check every label for acetaminophen or APAP.

**Is Fiorinal safer with alcohol than Fioricet?**

No. Fiorinal swaps acetaminophen for aspirin, but it still contains butalbital, so the dangerous sedation risk with alcohol is the same. Aspirin and alcohol together also raise the risk of stomach bleeding. Versions with codeine add an opioid and are even more dangerous with alcohol. Avoid alcohol with any butalbital product.

**Does the caffeine in Fioricet cancel out the drowsiness from alcohol?**

No. Caffeine can make you feel more alert, but it doesn't speed up how your body clears butalbital or alcohol, and it doesn't protect your breathing. Feeling more awake can make it harder to judge how impaired you are, which can lead to drinking more or driving when you shouldn't.

**Can DHM make it safe to drink on Fioricet?**

No. There's no good evidence that DHM or any other supplement reduces barbiturate sedation, protects breathing, or prevents acetaminophen liver damage. Don't use any supplement as a reason to drink while taking Fioricet, and ask your pharmacist before adding supplements to any prescription medicine.
